title: Threads and concurrency models
relevance: SDE interviews probe whether candidates understand shared-memory concurrency, user/kernel thread models, and hazards that show up in multithreaded server and runtime code.

phases.goal: Establish what a thread is, what it shares with siblings, and why threads are used despite concurrency hazards.

must_hit.point: A thread is the basic unit of CPU execution within a process — a single instruction sequence the scheduler can run independently; a process starts with one thread and may gain several that share the process memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines a thread as a schedulable instruction sequence inside a process and notes multiple threads share that process's memory.

must_hit.point: Threads share address space (text, data, heap), open files/sockets, globals/statics, signal handlers/accounting/PID; each keeps a private stack, registers (including SP), program counter, TID, scheduling state, and TLS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate correctly separates shared process-wide resources from per-thread private state, especially heap/globals vs stack/PC/registers.

must_hit.point: Shared heap and globals let threads communicate by reading/writing shared variables without IPC, but that shared writable state is what creates race conditions and motivates synchronization.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate links easy shared-variable communication to the danger of races.

must_hit.point: Threads buy responsiveness, easy resource sharing, economy vs processes, and multicore scalability; hazards include data races, deadlocks, oversubscription, and false sharing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists both benefits (e.g. UI stays live while a worker blocks) and named hazards like oversubscription or false sharing.

probes: What does a thread share with other threads in the same process, and what stays private?
Why use threads instead of processes, and what goes wrong when you do?

hints.1: Start from one process gaining several threads of execution.
hints.2: Contrast process-wide address space and descriptors with each thread's stack and registers.
hints.3: Shared heap/globals mean no IPC but also races; benefits are responsiveness/sharing/economy/scalability, costs are races/deadlocks/oversubscription/false sharing.

phases.goal: Explain user vs kernel threads, multithreading mapping models, concurrency vs parallelism, and Amdahl's bound.

must_hit.point: User-level threads are managed by a user library the kernel never sees (cheap switches, no mode switch) but a blocking syscall blocks the whole process; kernel-level threads are scheduled individually, can run on many cores, and a block affects only that thread at higher switch cost.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts who manages the threads, switch cost, blocking behavior, and multicore capability.

must_hit.point: Many-to-one maps many user threads to one kernel thread (cheap switches; blocking freezes all; no true multicore); one-to-one maps each user thread to its own kernel thread (true parallelism; creation is a kernel op with OS caps) and is today's default on Linux NPTL, Windows, and macOS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains both mappings and names one-to-one as the modern default on major OSes.

must_hit.point: Many-to-many maps many user threads onto a smaller pool of kernel threads (parallelism with bounded kernel overhead; complex two-level scheduling); two-level is many-to-many plus optional 1:1 bound threads for critical work.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes the pool mapping and optional binding, mentioning complexity as the cost.

must_hit.point: Concurrency is dealing with many tasks at once (structure; time-slicing on one core counts); parallelism is executing many tasks at the same instant and needs multiple cores — a single core can be concurrent but never truly parallel.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates interleaving/structure from simultaneous multicore execution, often with the chef analogy or equivalent.

must_hit.point: Amdahl's law: Speedup = 1 / ((1-P) + P/N); for a program that is 20% strictly sequential, as N goes to infinity speedup approaches 1/(1-P) = 1/0.2 = 5× — the serial fraction, not core count, is the ceiling.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states the formula or the 20% sequential → 5× max speedup interview result and names the serial fraction as the limit.

must_hit.point: The kernel tracks each thread with a TCB holding TID, saved registers, PC, stack pointer, state, and a pointer back to the process's PCB.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the TCB and lists key fields tying the thread to its PCB.

probes: What is the fatal flaw of pure user-level threads?
Max speedup of a program that is 20% strictly sequential, on 1000 cores?
How do many-to-one, one-to-one, and many-to-many map user threads to kernel threads?

hints.1: Ask who the kernel schedules: the process, or each thread.
hints.2: Walk blocking-syscall behavior, then the mapping table, then concurrency vs parallelism and Amdahl.
hints.3: User-level: blocking freezes all; one-to-one is today's default; concurrency ≠ parallelism; 20% sequential ⇒ 5× ceiling as N→∞.

phases.goal: Compare thread-management and mapping choices and the scale-vs-preemption trade of lightweight user-space threads.

must_hit.point: User-level threads trade very cheap switches for inability to use multiple cores and for whole-process stalls on any blocking call; kernel-level threads trade higher mode-switch cost for per-thread blocking and true multicore parallelism.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate frames the cost/benefit of each management layer without conflating them with mapping models.

must_hit.point: One-to-one gives true parallelism and isolated blocking but makes thread creation a kernel operation under OS count caps; many-to-many (and app-level thread pools) keep parallelism while bounding kernel overhead, at the cost of more complex scheduling.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts isolation/parallelism of 1:1 with bounded overhead and complexity of M:N / pools.

must_hit.point: Fibers, green threads, goroutines, virtual threads, and coroutines trade kernel preemption for enormous cheap concurrency by cooperative user-space scheduling that relies on tasks yielding (e.g. at I/O, channels, await/yield).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says scale comes from cooperative yielding onto few OS/carrier threads, at the cost of depending on yields.

probes: When would you prefer one-to-one over many-to-many (or a thread pool)?
What do goroutines or Java virtual threads give up to support huge numbers of concurrent tasks?

hints.1: Think about blocking calls and how many cores you need.
hints.2: Compare creation/switch cost and scheduling complexity across models.
hints.3: 1:1 isolates blocking and parallelizes; M:N/pools/goroutines/Loom bound OS threads but need cooperative yield.

phases.goal: Apply concurrency models to thread pools, safety/reentrancy/TLS, fork-in-multithreaded processes, and modern lightweight runtimes.

must_hit.point: A thread pool creates a fixed set of workers that wait on a shared work queue, pick up tasks, run them, and return — bounding concurrency and removing per-task creation latency (many-to-many at the application level).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes fixed workers + queue and names bounding concurrency / avoiding spawn-per-task cost.

must_hit.point: Thread-safe code behaves correctly under concurrent threads (locks, atomics, or no shared mutable state); reentrant code can be interrupted and re-entered safely with no static/global mutable state and no pointers to static data — all reentrant code is thread-safe, but not all thread-safe code is reentrant (a mutex-guarded function can self-deadlock if a signal handler re-enters it).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes the two and gives the mutex + signal-handler self-deadlock counterexample.

must_hit.point: If a thread in a multithreaded process calls fork, the child gets only the calling thread; mutexes held by vanished threads stay locked forever in the child, so the child should generally only exec or call async-signal-safe functions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states only the caller survives in the child and explains the locked-mutex hazard and exec/async-signal-safe guidance.

must_hit.point: TLS is data that looks global but has a private instance per thread (e.g. C errno, Java ThreadLocal); Go goroutines multiplex many-to-many onto a small OS-thread pool yielding at I/O/channels; Java virtual threads yield on blocking I/O onto few carriers; coroutines yield at explicit await/yield.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines TLS with an example and briefly describes at least one lightweight runtime's multiplexing/yield points.

probes: What happens if a thread in a multithreaded process calls fork?
Is every thread-safe function reentrant? Why or why not?
Why use a thread pool instead of spawning a thread per request?

hints.1: Consider what state exists after fork and what 'thread-safe' guarantees.
hints.2: fork copies only the caller; mutexes vs signal re-entry; pools bound workers on a queue.
hints.3: Child inherits only the forking thread so held locks stick; mutex-guarded code can self-deadlock on signal re-entry; pools reuse fixed workers.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: User-level threads switch very cheaply with no mode switch but cannot use multiple cores and any blocking syscall stalls the whole process; kernel-level threads cost a mode switch to schedule but block only the calling thread and run in parallel across cores.

One-to-one gives true parallelism and isolates blocking to one thread, but creation is a kernel operation under OS caps; many-to-many and application thread pools keep parallelism while bounding kernel/thread count and creation latency, at the cost of more complex two-level or queue-based scheduling.

tradeoffs.topic: Preemptive kernel threads vs cooperative lightweight threads
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Kernel-scheduled threads get preemption and OS-level isolation of blocking; fibers/green threads/goroutines/virtual threads/coroutines multiplex huge numbers onto few OS threads cheaply but depend on cooperative yields at I/O, channels, or await/yield points.

gotchas.trap: Assuming pure user-level threads can block in one thread while others keep running.
gotchas.correction: The kernel sees one process, so a blocking syscall blocks the entire process and every other user-level thread stalls with it.
Concurrency is dealing with many tasks at once (including time-slicing on one core); parallelism is executing many tasks at the same instant and requires multiple cores.

gotchas.trap: Expecting more cores to remove an Amdahl ceiling when much work is serial.
gotchas.correction: If 20% of work is strictly sequential, as N→∞ speedup approaches 1/0.2 = 5× — the serial fraction, not core count, is the limit.

gotchas.trap: Treating mutex-protected thread-safe code as reentrant.
gotchas.correction: All reentrant code is thread-safe, but a mutex-guarded function can self-deadlock if a signal handler re-enters it before the first call finishes.

gotchas.trap: Expecting fork in a multithreaded process to duplicate all threads cleanly.
gotchas.correction: The child gets only the calling thread; mutexes held by threads that vanish stay locked forever, so the child should generally only exec or use async-signal-safe functions.

gotchas.trap: Spawning an unbounded number of threads per task for scalability.
gotchas.correction: Per-task creation is expensive and can exhaust the system; oversubscription causes context-switch thrash — thread pools bound concurrency with a fixed worker set on a shared queue.
